$comment: Gameplay numbers. No tunable constant lives in a logic file; everything here is validated by schema at server start and can be hot reloaded from the admin page.

flight.$comment: Top speed and max turn rate follow from thrust-to-mass and torque-to-inertia on these curves, so a design's handling falls out of its layout rather than a per-hull table.

thrusters.$comment: A maneuvering thruster further from the centre of mass has more leverage. The reference arm sets how much layout matters: torque is strength * (1 + arm / referenceArm).

mass.$comment: Cargo and Propellant are carried mass, so a full hold flies worse than an empty one.

hull.$comment: A ship is written off when its bridge is destroyed or total structure falls below this share of its intact structure.

licences.$comment: Hull licences cap module count and grid extent. Named in spec section 7. Rank orders the ladder: a captain may buy any warrant above the one they hold, and the order is data rather than the order of keys in this file.

ports.$comment: What a berth charges for what is not a commodity. Propellant and Ordnance are commodities and are priced by the berth's own Staple, as spec section 9 requires; a fixed rate here meant a berth short of Propellant still sold it at the list price, and the same good had two prices.

start.$comment: What a captain is given when they are first entered in the Register, and where they are set down. Marks and the system can be overridden per server; the draught and the opening Ordnance are the game's own. Propellant is not listed because it is filled to whatever the draught's tanks hold: a new captain never reads a figure their hull cannot carry.

market.$comment: Price is the base price scaled by target over stock, raised to the elasticity, and clamped to the tier's band. Elasticity at 0.6 means a berth down to a quarter of its target quotes about 2.3x: enough that a shortage is worth flying to, not so much that one hold empties a berth's purse. The spread is what a berth keeps between what it pays and what it charges, and is what makes invariant 1 true: buying and selling back at one berth always loses it. Six per cent, with a landing fee of 25, because the starting draught carries twenty units: at twelve per cent and a fee of sixty, the costs of a leg exceeded the whole margin on a hold that size and the only possible trade was a losing one. The soak measured it.
market.$comment2: A berth wants targetHours of whatever it makes or eats on hand, never fewer than baselineTarget, and can hold capacityMultiple times that. Five days of throughput: a berth holding only hours of it empties between freight runs and spends its life at the price ceiling, which is not a market, and the time constant has to be long enough that a captain's hold is a nudge rather than a shock. A commodity a berth neither makes nor eats still trades, at the baseline: the berth is a market in it, just not a source or a sink.

freight.$comment: What the Reach's own freighters move, from surplus to shortage. Deliberately slower than a captain: an overused lane has to decay faster than the freighters repair it, and a rested one has to recover while nobody is looking. threshold is how far from target a berth must be before freight bothers with it, as a fraction: set wide on purpose, because freight that holds every berth within a few per cent of target leaves a captain nothing to carry. It is the floor under the economy, not its market maker, and the band it leaves open is the trade. and maxHops is how far a load will travel: the Reach is six lanes across, so freight can in principle reach anywhere, which it must, because Leaf is grown only in the Marque and chewed only in the Home Roads.

manufacturers.$comment: Who makes what. A module's name carries its maker in full, as a parts catalogue would; a narrow list shows the code instead and drops the prefix, so the part is readable rather than the firm.

yard.$comment: What a yard charges. The premium is insurance on the hull, added to what the modules cost; the refund is what a captain gets back for the marks value of modules stripped in a refit, which is deliberately half, because shipbuilding is the economy's main sink and a refit that paid for itself would not be one. Materials stripped come back in full: the yard has the parts in its hands. The claim is what insurance settles when a hull is written off, as a share of what its modules cost: half, so losing a hull costs a captain the better part of it, and the premium paid on every build is a fraction of that.
yard.$liveriesComment: A yard delivers a hull in one of these, chosen by the hull's own id so it is settled once and never changes. Free captains buy paint by the drum, not by the swatch: working greys, a weathered olive and an oxide red, all from the palette in docs/ART_DIRECTION.md.

law.$comment: What the Prize Court charges for firing on lawful traffic. A composition is struck per point of damage dealt — shields included, because the offence is the attack and not whether it got through — plus a flat sum for a hull written off, and both are weighted by how much law reaches the system: the Home Roads at full, the Concessions lightly, the Marque not at all. A posted captain is refused at Home Roads berths until it is paid.

world.$comment: spawnStandoff is how far off a berth a captain who has never flown, or who has just been written off, is set down: short enough that the berth is on screen and the landing prompt is already up, so the first thing a new captain sees is where they are. The Unlettered hold further out, in open space between the berths, and scatter about their anchor. Where a hull arrives from a lane comes from the system's own radius, not from here.

patrolsBySecurity.$comment: How many of the Prize Court's patrols stand in a system. They answer for the Home Roads and keep a thinner watch over the Concessions; the Marque has none.

raidersBySecurity.$comment: How many Unlettered hunt a system, by how much law reaches it. The Home Roads are patrolled, so nothing hunts there; the Marque is nobody's.

world.$rockComment: What a worked rock recovers in a day of world time. Slow enough that a belt is a place rather than a tap — a captain who strips a rock comes back to find it still thin — and fast enough that a belt somebody worked out a month ago is worth visiting again.

exchange.$comment: The Bourse. Spec section 10. A market tick is one pass of the house trader and one fold of the period's earnings into the smoothed figure; dividends fall on every dividendEvery-th tick.
exchange.$valueFloorComment: Marks a share at the smallest. A company that earns nothing for a while is cheap, not worthless, and a price of zero is a price no pool can quote out of.
exchange.$houseRateComment: Fraction of the gap to fair value the house trader covers each tick. At 0.12 a price is most of the way there in about twenty ticks, which is long enough for a captain to trade ahead of it and short enough that the news explains the move while it is still moving.
exchange.$holdingCapComment: Most of a company's float one captain may hold, so no one player can corner a listing — and the ceiling on what self-dealing could ever capture.
exchange.$maxPoolFractionComment: Most of a pool's shares one order may take. Without it a single order walks the curve to an absurd price and the next captain finds a market that cannot be traded.
exchange.$invariant6Comment: smoothing * multiple * holdingCap must stay below 1, or self-dealing pays: a captain could buy shares, spend to lift that company's earnings, and sell for more than they spent. At 0.02 * 400 * 0.10 = 0.8 they recover at most eighty marks of share value per hundred spent, before the Staple's spread and the Bourse's own fees. The content loader refuses to start if this is violated.
exchange.$multipleComment: Marks of value per mark of earnings a tick. Large because a tick is twenty seconds and a company is worth rather more than twenty seconds of trading; fairValue divides by the float, so this is a company-wide figure and not a price.
exchange.$earningsFloorComment: A company is never worth nothing. Smoothed earnings never fall below this fraction of what the company opened on, because a quiet quarter does not sell the yards: there is still a going concern underneath. Without it a listing whose earnings depend on player orders alone — Slipway, which earns only on its fittings — decays to the value floor within a day of nobody building, and then spikes many times over on the next hull. A quarter leaves a bad year costing three quarters of the share price, which is a drawdown and not a collapse.

standing.$comment: What a captain is worth to each of the three companies. Spec section 11: a standing responds to what they do and affects port access, prices and which commissions they are offered. It is not experience: it can fall as fast as it rises, and it is held per company, so pleasing one costs with the others.
standing.$refusedBelowComment: A berth closes to a captain this far out of favour. Low enough that it takes a campaign to reach, not one bad afternoon.
standing.$discountComment: Standing shades the Staple's spread in a captain's favour, up to this fraction, so a regular is worth being. Half the spread, not all of it: invariant 1 says buying and selling back at one berth loses money, and a discount that merely matched the spread would make the round trip free for a favoured captain, which is the same hole one step smaller.
standing.$rivalShareComment: A gain with one company costs this fraction of it with each of the other two, which at a half makes standing zero-sum across the three charters: working all three in rotation nets exactly nothing. Below a half it does not — at 0.4 a captain gains a fifth of every push and ends up well in with everybody, which is the one state the setting cannot have.
standing.$decayComment: Standing drifts back toward nothing when a captain stops dealing with a company at all, so an old grudge and an old favour both fade.

letters.$comment: Monopoly goods and letters of marque, as spec section 19 describes them. The monopolies bind only in the Home Roads; outside them there is no contraband at all, because there is nobody to enforce it.
letters.$goodStandingComment: Standing with the holder at which carrying its monopoly good through the Home Roads stops being smuggling. A captain the company deals with is a captain it licenses.
letters.$scanChanceComment: Chance a patrol scans a hull it passes close to. Not every hull every time: smuggling that is always caught is not a decision.
letters.$costComment: What a letter costs at a company's seat.
letters.$lapsesComment: A letter lapses if standing with its issuer falls this low. It is a company's instrument, not a possession.
letters.$standingCostComment: Taking a letter costs this much standing with each of the other two charters, at once. It is a declaration.
letters.$prizePremiumComment: What prize cargo fetches above the quote at the issuer's berths. Well below the half of a hold that is lost when a hull is destroyed, so a capture staged between friends loses money — which is the whole reason the number is small.
